description:
AstroPy is a team of students from Cairo, Egypt, who love space, science and building creative projects. We believe the best way to make people curious about space is to tell its stories in a way anyone can enjoy.

For this challenge, we want to bring the story of NASA's abandoned equipment on the Moon and Mars to life for kids and students, showing that every machine left behind still has something to teach us.

Meet the crew

• Moaz Mohamed AboElfetoh — Code development

• Mariam Waleed — UI/UX design

• Ziad Ashraf — Graphic design

• Salma Khaled Elsayed — 3D models and AR

• Rana Fayez — Data collection from NASA and NSSDCA sources

• Mohamed Nabil Fawzy — Testing

Six students from Cairo, one mission: every story, fact check and design decision in AstroTales was made together.
summary: We built AstroTales, a free web game where the machines NASA left on the Moon, Mars and in deep space tell kids aged 8-12 their own stories. It answers the challenge directly: 14 real NASA machines, from the Eagle lander to Opportunity and Kepler, each speak in first person through short Story cards with voice and subtitles. Kids then play a mini-game based on the real mission, prove what they learned with "Fact or Cap?" cards, and see the machine in 3D, or in their own room in AR. What sets it apart is trust: every fact links to its NASA source (NSSDCA and science.nasa.gov), and the app uses 28 NASA photos and 9 NASA 3D models. Nothing is invented. No ads, no accounts, no personal data: one link, any phone. Their missions ended. Their stories didn't.
details:
What happens to a robot when its mission ends?

NASA has left dozens of machines across the solar system: landers on the Moon, rovers on Mars, probes still drifting into deep space. Their missions are over, and most kids have never heard of them. AstroTales gives them their voices back.

The machines tell their own stories

The child becomes an astronaut. They pick a character, launch from Earth, fly through a 3D solar system and land at real sites on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. There they meet 14 NASA machines: Eagle, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Kepler, Dawn, Pioneer 10 and more. Each one tells its story in first person, with voice and typed subtitles, as four short Story cards.

Learn by playing the real mission

After the story, the child plays the machine's real job: land the lunar module, wipe the dust off Opportunity's solar panels, or hunt for planets like Kepler. A treasure chest opens only after they answer "Fact or Cap?" cards correctly. Completing a world earns coins and unlocks the next.

Bring NASA hardware into your room

Each machine has a profile with real facts, NASA photos and source links. 11 of them can be viewed in 3D and placed in the child's room in augmented reality, using NASA's own 3D models.

The difference: every fact comes from NASA

Facts without a source do not ship. Every profile links back to the official NASA record (NSSDCA and science.nasa.gov), so the story is the machine's voice and the profile is the official science. "Fact or Cap?" goes further and teaches media literacy: kids learn that Opportunity's viral "my battery is low" line was a poetic translation of its data, not its real words.

How we checked the facts

1. Every fact has a source. Each fact on a machine's profile links to the NASA or NSSDCA page it came from. Facts without a source do not ship.

2. Numbers come from the record. Dates, counts and catalog IDs (for example NSSDCA 1969-099C) are taken from the NSSDCA Master Catalog and NASA mission pages.

3. Every story line is checked against its source. The story is the machine's voice, so each line was compared with the sourced facts before it shipped. Where a famous quote is not literal, like Opportunity's "my battery is low", Fact or Cap says so.

Built for how kids watch today

Gen Alpha grew up on short, swipeable content, so we don't fight the scroll, we give it a destination. Each card is under 10 seconds and 20 words; each machine takes about two minutes. Phones get a full-screen Stories view, laptops a game scene, both from the same content.

Safe and open for every classroom

No ads, no streaks, no loot boxes, no accounts, no personal data, no backend. Large touch targets, readable contrast, reduced-motion support and a typeface made for young readers. One link, no sign-up, no install: ready for classrooms, museums and outreach events. Each machine is a single content file, so new missions and languages can be added without new code.

Who it helps

• Kids aged 8–12: short Story cards, real missions to play, and a "Fact or Cap?" habit of asking what is real.

• Teachers and classrooms: one link, no sign-up or install, about two minutes per machine, so it fits into a lesson.

• Museums and outreach events: works on any phone or laptop, with no accounts and no personal data.

• NASA's archive: NSSDCA records, mission pages, photos and 3D models reach an audience that would never open them, and every profile links back to the source.

How AstroTales can last

• Free for kids, always. No ads, no in-app purchases, no data to sell.

• Almost no running cost. It is a static website with no backend or accounts, so hosting stays near zero as more kids play.

• Schools and teachers: classroom packs with lesson plans and printable cards, sold to schools or funded by education programs.

• Museums and planetariums: licensed exhibit and kiosk versions for space exhibitions and outreach events.

• Grants and sponsors: STEM-education grants and space-industry sponsors fund new machines and languages.

• Cheap to grow: each new machine is one content file, so adding missions (or partner content) costs little.

Built with

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, GSAP (animation), three.js (3D solar system), Google model-viewer (3D and AR, with Draco-compressed NASA models), Howler.js and the Web Audio API (sound), Zustand (progress saved in the browser) and Vercel (hosting). Source code (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/Moaz-Sakrr/AstroTales

What's next

An Arabic version (all text is stored separately so it can be translated), testing in classrooms with teachers, and more NASA machines, each added as one content file.

Their missions ended. Their stories didn't.

Project showcase: one kid's journey through AstroTales

1. Start your mission: postcards from the Moon

2. Blast off from Earth

3. Fly through a real 3D solar system

4. Head for the Moon

5. Follow the trail of real landing sites

6. The machines tell their own stories

7. On phones, stories play like the apps kids already know

8. Play the real mission: land the Eagle

9. Fact or Cap? Prove what you learned

10. Earn the machine's collectible card

11. Every fact links to its NASA source

12. From the screen to your room: NASA's Ingenuity in AR

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Claude Code (Anthropic): coding assistant for the web app and the demo video code. ElevenLabs: SI-generated voices for the machine characters. ChatGPT: our team hand-sketched the kid astronaut, then used ChatGPT to render the final character art; ChatGPT also rendered the device characters (Ingenuity, Pathfinder, InSight, Viking 1 and Surveyor 3) from our sketches and NASA photos. Gemini: generated the device card art. SI also helped draft story lines, which we then checked against the NASA sources. The cards and the kid's poses carry an "SI-generated" label in the app, and the demo video and the showcase images are labelled too. All facts come from the NASA sources listed below; SI did not write or invent any fact. No NASA logos, insignia or mission patches appear in any SI-generated image. SI sped up the work, but the story, the research and every design decision were made by our team.
